source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) The Art of Knowing When to Stop: optimal stopping in people and machines
finding: LLMs played a finite-horizon fuse-or-extract stopping game (combinatorial innovation) that humans also played. With direct play, LLM behaviour differed from both humans and the rational switch point.
numbers: Human baseline (Zhao, Velez, Griffiths 2024): 210 people, 4 conditions (p in {0.8,0.2}, w in {3,1.5}), 7 scored 10-step rounds; only 32% (HH) and 18% (LL) switched at the optimal step. GPT-3.5 switch-once rate: HH 71.4%, HL 14.3%, LH 57.1%, LL 28.6% (humans about 80%).
limits: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, Llama-3.1-70B. Small preliminary test.
agent_relevance: A bare LLM stopping judgement cannot be trusted; check it against the closed-form optimum.

source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) direct play detail
finding: Where humans stopped exploring too early (HH, HL, LH), LLMs stopped even earlier. In low-p-low-w, where the optimum is to extract from step 0, LLMs over-explored.
numbers: HH optimum step 9: GPT-4 and Llama-3.1 switched at step 5. HL optimum 7: GPT-4 step 5, Llama step 6. LH: GPT-4 step 6, Llama step 2. LL optimum 0: GPT-4 step 5, Llama step 3.
limits: Modal switch steps only; no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: LLM stopping errors go both ways, so one fixed correction (always search more) will not work.

source: Zhang and Zhao (2024) prompting effects
finding: Giving the formula plus an example optimal play (MDP prompt) was not enough. Adding a request to explain why the example is optimal (CoT prompt) moved models to the optimal switch point.
numbers: With CoT: GPT-3.5 peaked at optimal step 9 in HH; Llama-3.1 at optimal step 7 in HL and LH; in LL both prompts gave extraction at all 10 steps. Optimal from round 1 but drifting later: no learning across rounds, unlike humans.
limits: Heatmaps and qualitative description; few runs.
agent_relevance: Show a worked example with the reason, not only the equation.

source: Kalayci, Raman, Dughmi (2025) Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
finding: Each LLM generation is a costly box in Pandora's Box. A UCB-style algorithm learns stopping thresholds without knowing the reward distribution and is provably close to Weitzman's optimal rule.
numbers: Same quality as non-adaptive Best-of-N with 15-35% fewer generations on average (AlpacaFarm, HH-RLHF); savings rise from 15% to 35% as the target acceptance rate rises above 0.75.
limits: Quality measured by reward models, a proxy; offline simulation.
agent_relevance: Direct use of search theory in an LLM loop: decide when to stop sampling.

source: Kalayci et al. (2025) profit and win-rate experiments
finding: Under equal budgets the adaptive stopper beats non-adaptive Best-of-N; gains are largest when cost is low or budgets are high.
numbers: Llama-3.1 8B, Mistral-Instruct-v0.3 7B, Qwen-2.5 7B with two reward models gave 1,600 generation profiles. Win rate above 54% across most cost settings (c from 1e-5 to 1e-3; 100 random orderings; ties half credit). Cost-to-utility ratios 0.002 to 0.0002.
limits: Small open models only; adaptive method beats the best fixed N 'in nearly all cases', not all.
agent_relevance: Adaptive depth beats fixed depth even when fixed depth is tuned.

source: Kalayci et al. (2025) reward scaling and premature stopping
finding: Reward scores are not comparable across prompts, so a Bradley-Terry style transform converts them to an acceptance rate. Without an optimism (UCB) estimate the algorithm stops too early.
numbers: Acceptance-rate computation reaches under 1% relative error using 5000 intervals.
limits: Premature stopping appears when the tail is estimated from few samples.
agent_relevance: Keep an exploration bonus; do not stop after very few looks.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample reasoning paths in windows and stop as soon as a window is unanimous. A simple sequential stopping rule for self-consistency.
numbers: Average number of samples cut: MATH 33.8%, GSM8K 80.1%, StrategyQA 76.8%, CommonsenseQA 78.5%, Coin Flip 84.2%, Last Letters 67.4%, with comparable accuracy. Window size 8 in the main tables.
limits: GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Llama-2 7b; smallest savings on hardest task (MATH).
agent_relevance: Stop sampling when the first window agrees; keep going when it disagrees.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC versus equal-cost self-consistency
finding: Plain self-consistency with the same smaller sample count (L-hat) loses accuracy, while ESC keeps it. ESC also composes with other prompting methods.
numbers: In one plug-in test ESC beat CoT by 9.84% (PHP by 9.25%) with fewer samples. Weaker models lose more accuracy under L-hat-SC.
limits: Table rows were garbled in text extraction; abstract figures are the reliable ones.
agent_relevance: Spend saved budget on hard items.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 mostly fail to explore in multi-armed bandits. Only GPT-4 with a hint to explore, history summarised externally into per-arm averages, and zero-shot CoT worked.
numbers: Basic GPT-4 prompt: suffix failure (never picks the best arm again after some round) in more than 60% of replicates. Baselines 1000 replicates; GPT-3.5 N=20 over 48 prompt configurations; GPT-4 10 configurations on the hard instance.
limits: Small replicate counts for LLMs; simple K-armed instance. Same prompt without external summary fails.
agent_relevance: Give the agent per-option summary statistics instead of raw history.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) failure modes and hard instance
finding: Two failure modes: suffix failures (greedy-like lock-in) and uniform behaviour (all arms picked near-equally). Few GPT-4 configurations avoided suffix failures.
numbers: Hard instance, T=100: median reward UCB 0.55, Thompson 0.47, Greedy 0.40; one LLM config 0.68 with suffix-failure frequency at T/2 of 0.30; config BNRND suffix failures 0.00 but median reward 0.33.
limits: Avoiding lock-in cost reward when the model dithered.
agent_relevance: Track both lock-in and dithering in any search loop.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 handled vignette decisions well and beat humans on a bandit task by regret, but showed no directed exploration and ignored the time horizon.
numbers: Horizon task: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878) = -5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference, t(5566) = -0.043. Long horizon: humans improved more within a task, final regret slightly (n.s.) lower, t(5550) = -0.75.
limits: GPT-3 only, 2022; human data from an earlier study.
agent_relevance: Models do not value information for itself; tell the agent how many looks remain.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) directed versus random exploration
finding: A regression on the first free choice found GPT-3 random exploration did not depend on horizon and showed no directed exploration.
numbers: No significant interaction of reward difference by horizon; no positive effect of information difference.
limits: Newer models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Add an explicit value-of-information step before a costly look.

source: Jain and Krishnamurthy (2025) Interacting LLM agents: Bayesian social learning
finding: Optimal stopping controls herding in sequential LLM agents. The optimal policy is a threshold switching curve in belief space (Theorem 3); herding occurs in finite time (Theorem 2).
numbers: Experiments with Llama-3 on hate-speech classification and AAPL news (16 binary features) estimate the curve by policy gradient.
limits: Theory heavy; real LLM tests are small. Needs structural assumptions S1-S4.
agent_relevance: Let agents share private evidence until the public belief is strong enough.

source: Jain and Krishnamurthy (2025) model switching as stopping
finding: Switching from a large costly LLM to a small cheap one is framed as an optimal stopping problem on the accuracy-cost trade-off.
numbers: No single headline number; a more accurate LLM delays herding but costs more per use.
limits: General solution hard, so a threshold structure is assumed.
agent_relevance: Escalate to a stronger model only when a belief threshold says so.

source: Pilditch (2026) Knowing when to stop: Bayesian optimal stopping for LLM evaluations (optstop)
finding: Precision-based adaptive stopping for LLM evaluations: keep sampling uncertain items, stop where estimates are precise or stable.
numbers: On a 200-item, 10-epoch run it removed 57% to 97% of planned trials across 9 settings; mean efficiency gain 81.1%; mean absolute score deviation 0.006 on a 0-1 scale.
limits: Illustrative run; binary model coverage about 80% at 94% nominal under moderate heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Our own benchmark runs can stop early when estimates are tight.

source: Pilditch (2026) optstop safeguards and pathways
finding: A safeguard samples more cautiously as performance nears zero because rare successes matter. Continuous scores give the largest savings.
numbers: Continuous pathway mean saving 95.1%; mid-ordinal 57.2%; low-continuous 97.3%. Low-performance threshold default 1%.
limits: Savings depend on evaluation design; near-boundary performance can break intervals.
agent_relevance: Take more looks when the target event is rare.

source: Goldstein, McAfee, Suri, Wright (2020) Learning When to Stop Searching
finding: People learn near-optimal stopping in a repeated secretary problem; behaviour best fit by multiple-threshold models that include the optimal strategy. Human baseline for LLM tests.
numbers: 6,537 players, 48,336 games (7.39 per player). Optimal win rates: known distribution 0.622 (7 boxes), 0.599 (15 boxes); classic unknown 0.414 and 0.389. Win rates rose about 25 points over 10 games, within 5-10 points of the optimum.
limits: Online sample; game 1 best fit by a value-oblivious model; early errors mostly stopping too late.
agent_relevance: Humans learn in about 5-9 games; CoT-prompted LLMs start optimal and then drift.

source: Goldstein et al. (2020) thresholds
finding: Early players stopped about 25% of the time below the critical value and up to 75% above it. By game 4 all 7-box threshold intervals contained the optimum.
numbers: Optimal critical percentiles, 7 boxes, boxes remaining 1 to 7: 0, 0.50, 0.690, 0.776, 0.825, 0.856, 0.878. Search depth fell about a third of a box over 5 games.
limits: Some intervals missed in games 5-8; all contained the optimum again by game 9.
agent_relevance: A stopping rule can be a table of thresholds by looks remaining.

source: Seong (2025) Heuristic Solutions for the Best Secretary Problem
finding: Five adaptive heuristics update stopping thresholds as data arrive; simulation shows they match or beat classical rules in stability.
numbers: Five rules; simple expected-record rule strong; ensemble most consistent.
limits: Abstract page only read; simulation only; no LLM.
agent_relevance: Use an ensemble of cheap stopping rules.

source: Rapoport, Seale, Spiliopoulos (2023) Progressive stopping heuristics
finding: Descriptive heuristics work only when the optimum is a single threshold. A heuristic using the ratio of interviewed to remaining applicants works across many multi-threshold variants and a competitive variant.
numbers: Abstract-level: near-optimal performance in a competitive secretary problem with several employers.
limits: Only the abstract and first page read; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Stop when fraction seen exceeds a rising rule as options run out.

source: Marcu and Noussair (2022) Sequential search with a price freeze option (working paper)
finding: Lab experiment: treatment effects matched an optimal-search model. Regret, sunk-cost, misperceived horizon and risk aversion did not improve the fit.
numbers: Varied whether freezing is possible, its cost, and the horizon.
limits: Abstract and first page read; no URL known; keywords include under-searching.
agent_relevance: Optimal search describes humans fairly well when the task is clear.

source: Kleinberg, Waggoner, Weyl (2016) Descending Price Optimally Coordinates Search
finding: Dutch auctions coordinate costly search better than English or simultaneous auctions because the price is guaranteed when information is acquired.
numbers: Calibrations to start-up acquisition and timber auctions: coordination losses are one to two orders of magnitude larger than ex-ante asymmetry losses.
limits: Theory; no LLM. Pandora's Box lineage.
agent_relevance: In multi-agent search, fix the budget before agents spend effort.

source: Weitzman (1979) Optimal search for the best alternative
finding: Pandora's Box: compute a reservation value per option, open in that order, stop when the best found beats all remaining reservation values.
numbers: Cited by Kalayci et al. as the optimal known-distribution strategy.
limits: Not opened; known from citation only.
agent_relevance: Compute a reservation value per option.

source: Wilson et al. (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: Source of the horizon task used by Binz and Schulz; humans seek information more when the horizon is long.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Cited only.
agent_relevance: Human directed-exploration baseline.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Fixed-N majority vote over sampled reasoning paths; the fixed-budget method that ESC and adaptive stopping improve on.
numbers: Not opened; cited by Li et al. and Kalayci et al.
limits: Fixed budget wastes samples on easy items.
agent_relevance: Baseline for stopping rules.

source: Koopman (1956) and Stone (1975) classical search theory
finding: Classical operations-research search theory: allocate search effort over cells to maximise detection probability per cost.
numbers: Not opened; named in the subfield brief.
limits: No LLM work using it was found.
agent_relevance: Background lineage.
